editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We present a tiling of more than 99.985698\% of the Euclidean plane with six colors, reducing the previous record for uncovered fraction of the plane by about 12.8\%. We also present a tiling of more than 95.99\% of the plane with five colors. It is thus shown that any unit-distance graph of order at most 6992 and 24 in the plane can be properly 6-colored and 5-colored, respectively.

editorial_contributions.text: It has been well-known that given a tiling of the plane with regular hexagons of diameter 1 (more properly, infinitesimally less than 1), the hexagons can be colored with 7 colors, such that no unit distance occurs between points of identically colored hexagons. Furthermore, there is a small \textit{interval}, namely \([1, \sqrt{7}/2)\), such that numbers from this interval do not occur as distances between points of identically colored hexagons. A similar question can be asked for \(k\geq 7\)-colorations of the hexagons: what is the largest possible \(d(k)\), such that for some \(k\)-coloration of the hexagons, no number from the interval \([1,d(k))\) appears as a distance between points of identically colored hexagons. For \(k>7\) the exact value of \(d(k)\) is not known, although estimates exists. The paper under review studies tilings with congruent, but not regular hexagons of diameter 1, and achieves somewhat bigger intervals, whose elements do not occur as distances between points of identically colored hexagons, than what was achieved for colorations of tilings with regular hexagons of diameter 1.

editorial_contributions.text:
The present second edition of this popular book for talented high school students and also for mathematicians contains mostly the material of the first edition. The contents of the first edition is outlined in the report (1991; Zbl 0727.52001).

The second edition is expanded by the following five short chapters. Chapter 5 (five pages) recalls two theorems by \textit{D. Karabash} [Geombinatorics 16, No.~2, 262--265 (2006)] on rectangles that can be tiled by L-tetrominoes of the same orientation in such a way that the tiling has \(2\)-fold symmetry. Chapter 6 (five pages) presents some results on three-dimensional tromino tilings of a cube obtained mostly by \textit{N. Starr} [Geombinatorics 18, No.~2, 72--87 (2008; Zbl 1184.05020)]. Chapter 7 (four pages) comments some results on the Ramsey number \(R(m,n)\), first of all the result by \textit{B. D. McKay} and \textit{S. P. Radziszowski} that \(R(4,5) = 25\) [J. Graph Theory 19, No.~3, 309--322 (1995; Zbl 0822.05050)], and also the estimates \(43 \leq R(5,5) \leq 49\) with the conjecture that \(R(5,5) =43\). See \textit{G. Exoo} [J. Graph Theory 13, No.~1, 97--98 (1989; Zbl 0661.05044)] and \textit{B. D. McKay} and \textit{S. P. Radziszowski} [J. Comb. Theory, Ser. B 69, No.~2, 193--209 (1997; Zbl 0860.05043)].

Chapter 8 (four pages) gives information on the progress in the research on the famous Borsuk problem after the first edition of this book; the story of finding counterexamples. Starting from the well-nown result by \textit{J. Kahn} and \textit{G. Kalai} [Bull. Am. Math. Soc., New Ser. 29, No.~1, 60--62 (1993; Zbl 0786.52002)] and finishing by the result of \textit{A. Hinrichs} and \textit{C. Richter} [Discrete Math. 270, No.~1--3, 137--147 (2003; Zbl 1028.52012)] on the counterexample in \(E^{298}\), which (till now) is the space of the lowest known dimension for which the Borsuk problem has a negative solution. 

Chapter 9 (twelve pages) discusses the following problem of E. Nelson (1950): which is the smallest number \(\chi\) of colours sufficient for colouring the plane in such a way that no two points of the same colour lie apart at unit distance. After recalling the proofs by E. Nelson (1950) and J. Isbell (1950) that \(4 \leq \chi \leq 7\), the author presents results on the \(n\)-colouring of a given type and on the almost chromatic number \(\chi_a\); see the paper by \textit{I. Hoffman} and \textit{A. Soifer} [Geombinatorics 3, No.~2, 38--40 (1993; Zbl 0845.05037)].

editorial_contributions.text:
For twenty five years Martin Gardner produced the celebrated mathematical games monthly columns for \textit{Scientific American}. Nobody managed to fit his shoes ever since. This is why it has been a special joy to see these columns expanded with a wealth of new results and appear in the form of books. 


This is at least the fifteenth such collection. As Martin Gardner put it in introduction, ``This is a book of mathematical jokes, if `joke' is taken in a sense broad enough to include any kind of mathematics that is mixed with a strong element of fun.'' It consists of twenty essays, all deep and all entertaining. Once challenged, the reader is afforded the pleasure of working on several problems on his own. The reader can then compare his discoveries with the \textit{answers}, that follow each essay. These answers will definitely inspire many readers to do further reading and investigations on their own. 


The readers of the `Four color map theorem' chapter, may wish to study a new proof of the theorem, obtained in 1994 by the group of four mathematicians (one per color ?) \textit{Neal Robertson}, \textit{Daniel P. Sanders}, \textit{Paul D. Seymour}, and \textit{Robin Thomas}. Their manuscript ``The four-colour theorem'' has been accepted for publication in J. Combin. Theory, Ser. B. 


One of the problems asks to cut a given triangle \(ABC\) with an obtuse angle \(B\) into seven acute triangles. Here is a simple universal solution (for all obtuse triangles): inscribe a circle \(S\) in \(ABC\); draw tangent lines to \(S\) that cut off \(ABC\) two acute triangles that contain the angles \(A\) and \(C\); and connect the vertices of the remaining pentagon to the center of \(S\). 


This is my favorite of the many wonderful Martin Gardner's books. Not just young and not so young mathematicians: every curious person should enjoy reading these essays and pondering on issues and problems they raise. One of those is this reviewer's favorite open problem in all of mathematics (p. 123): 


How many colors are required for coloring the plane so that no two points, a unit distance apart, lie on the same color? 


The answer is known to be 4, 5, 6 or 7: a vast spread, especially since the problem was created by a young University of Chicago student, Edward Nelson, long time ago, in 1950. Nelson was 18 years old then!

editorial_contributions.text:
Paul Erdős asked me once whether I read ``The Book.'' ``Of course not,'' answered I, thinking that Paul referred, as he often did, to God's created ``transfinite book that contained all problems and their best solutions.'' ``Call [Willy] Moser, he will send you a copy,'' Erdős said. This is how I received my first of many versions of ``Research Problems in Discrete Geometry.''

The history of The Book deserves its own book. The famous problem poser and solver Leo Moser started it 1963, with his own 50 open problems. The flame was kept alive by his younger brother and coauthor Willy Moser, who was joined by János Pach in 1986, and by Peter Brass in 2000. Looking at many versions of The Book in front of me, I see how wonderfully the book has grown. It now includes over 500 open problems of discrete geometry, many more than any book on the subject that I know. Yet, The Book retains the attraction of its earlier versions: the problems are very contagious, easy to understand, yet hard to solve, especially to solve completely.

Contents include Density Problems for Packings and Coverings; Structural Packing and Covering Problems; Packing and Covering with Homothetic Copies; Tiling Problems; Distance Problems; Problems on Repeated Subconfigurations; Incidence and Arrangement Problems; Problems on Points in General Position; Graph Drawing and Geometric Graphs; Lattice Point Problems; and Geometric Inequalities. 

At the age of computing and information, it is only natural that discrete mathematics is flourishing. It is therefore natural that the authors could not include all aspect of discrete geometry in one book. They chose areas close to them, and left to others to write about such exciting areas of discrete geometry as convex polytopes, Helly-type problems, stochastic geometry, etc.

The book is written in the style of Paul Erdős's problem articles. It is fitting therefore that The Book includes Paul's introduction written for an earlier version. Each section is a self-contained essay that provides the history of a problem, known partial results, motivation and bibliography -- everything needed for the reader, especially a young mathematician seeking a problem to conquer, to start his or her research. Professionals will find The Book to be a valuable encyclopedic source for their research. Indeed, this is an exceptional book, a must for all active mathematicians.

The review would be incomplete without a sample problem. I choose, quite subjectively, my favorite unsolved problem in all of mathematics (Problem 1, section 5.9): What is the minimum number of colors for coloring the points of the plane so that no two points at unit distance receive the same color?

The last words of Paul Erdős's introduction are: ``I wish the reader good luck with the solutions!'' I can only add, Amen.

editorial_contributions.text:
This very nicely presented book, lovingly prepared by the author over a period of 18 years, studies problems involving colored objects, and the Ramsey theory that such problems are imbedded into. Two problems receiving special attention are the well-known four color problem (resolved in 1976 after an assault of 124 years) and the author's ``favorite open problem in mathematics'', the chromatic number of the plane problem: What is the smallest number of colors sufficient for coloring the plane so that no two points of the same color are unit distance apart? The book is very thorough, in unusual ways perhaps best expressed by the author himself: 


 
``This book includes not just mathematics, but also the process of investigation, trains of mathematical thought, and where possible, psychology of mathematical invention. The book does not just include history and prehistory of Ramsey theory and related fields, but also conveys the process of historical investigation -- the kitchen of historical research if you will. It has captivated me, and made me feel like a Sherlock Holmes -- I hope my reader will enjoy this sense of suspense and discovery as much as I have. \dots I hope the book will present mathematics as a human endeavor: the reader should expect to find in it not only results, but also portraits of their creators; not only mathematical facts, but also open problems; not only new mathematical research, but also new historical investigations; not only mathematical aspirations, but also moral dilemmas of the times between and during the two horrific World Wars of the twentieth century.''


 
For example, new facts and artifacts are presented, pertaining to the lives of Issai Schur, Pierre Joseph Henry Baudet, and Bartel Leendert van der Waerden. The 49 chapters are divided into 11 parts: I. Merry-go-round; II. Colored plane; III. Coloring graphs; IV. Coloring maps (a map is defined to be a plane connected multigraph with no bridges); V. Colored graphs; VI. The Ramsey principle; VII. Colored integers: Ramsey theory before Ramsey and its aftermath; VIII. Colored polygons: Euclidean Ramsey theory; IX. Colored integers in service of chromatic number of the plane; X. Predicting the future (here the author conjectures that the chromatic number of the plane is either 4 or 7, expressing a preference for 7); XI. Farewell to the reader. There are an extensive bibliography, and indices of names, subjects, and notations; the latter two are brief. The author has used his own book as a text, at both the senior and the graduate level. There are numerous open problems, but no formal problem sets. But there is much to recommend this book, both for mathematicians and for those who wish to learn more about mathematicians and their subject.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The Hadwiger-Nelson problem asks for the minimum number of colors required to color the plane such that if two points are unit distance apart from each other, then those points have different colors \textit{H. T. Croft} et al. [Unsolved problems in geometry. New York etc.: Springer-Verlag (1991; Zbl 0748.52001)]. It has been shown that the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane is 5, 6, or 7 (see [H. T. Croft, loc. cit.] and [\textit{A. De Grey}, ``The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1804.02385}]). Versions of this problem for the hyperbolic plane are investigated in [\textit{E. De Corte} and \textit{K. Golubev}, ``Lower bounds for the measurable chromatic number of the hyperbolic plane'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1708.01081}] and [\textit{H. Parlier} and \textit{C. Petit}, ``Chromatic numbers for the hyperbolic plane and discrete analogs'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1701.08648}]. In this paper, we answer this question for the Taxicab plane. In particular, we show that the minimum number of colors necessary to color the Taxicab plane such that no two points unit distance apart have the same color is four. We do this by tiling the plane using taxicab circles, all of which have radius \(r=1/2\). All the points in the interior of a given circle are colored using the same color. However, the interiors of adjacent circles are colored using different colors, and the boundary of each circle is colored using all four of the colors. This is done in such a way that points on opposite sides of a circle are colored using different colors.
